definition: A 3PL (third-party logistics provider) is an outside company that stores a brand's inventory and packs and ships its orders.
A person who invests their own money in very early companies, usually in exchange for a small share of ownership.
B2B (business-to-business) means selling to other businesses rather than to individual consumers.
Building a company with the founders' own money and the cash the business earns, rather than raising money from outside investors.
An outside sales agent who pitches a brand's products to store buyers and is usually paid a commission on sales.
The amount of money a company loses each month when it spends more than it brings in.
CAC (customer acquisition cost) is the average amount a business spends on marketing and sales to win one new customer.
A table showing who owns what share of a company, including founders, investors, and employees.
A scheduled period, often once a year, when a store chain's buyer decides which products to add to or drop from a section of the store.
The share of customers or subscribers who stop buying or cancel over a period of time.
A product made with a short list of simple, recognizable ingredients and no artificial additives.
A co-packer, also called a co-man (co-manufacturer), is an outside factory that makes and packages products for a brand under the brand's name.
COGS (cost of goods sold) is the direct cost to make or buy the products a company sells, including ingredients, materials, packaging, and factory labor, but not rent, salaries, or marketing.
A group of customers who started buying in the same period, tracked together to see how their buying changes over time.

What is left from a sale after paying for the product and the costs that rise with each order, such as shipping, packaging, and payment fees. It shows how much each sale adds toward covering fixed costs and profit.
Mainstream supermarket chains such as Kroger or Albertsons, as opposed to natural or specialty stores.
CPG (consumer packaged goods) refers to products sold in packages to everyday shoppers, such as food, drinks, and personal care items.
Handing out free samples in a store so shoppers can try a product.
The drop in each existing owner's percentage of a company when new shares are issued, for example to new investors.
DTC (direct-to-consumer) means selling straight to customers, usually through the brand's own website, instead of through stores or other middlemen.
The research an investor or buyer does on a company before investing in it or buying it.
Ownership in a company. Giving up equity means selling part of the business to investors or giving it to employees.
The sale of a company, or its listing on the stock market, which lets founders and investors turn their ownership into cash.
A cycle where each part of the business feeds the next, so growth builds on itself over time.
Free product a brand gives a retailer to stock the shelves for a new item, a common form of slotting fee.
An early round of money raised from people the founder already knows, usually before professional investors get involved.
The plan for how a company will launch a product and reach its first customers, including who to sell to, where, and at what price.
The share of each sale left over after paying the direct cost of making the product. If a $10 item costs $4 to make, the gross margin is 60%.
How long it takes from placing an order with a supplier to receiving the goods.
LTV (lifetime value) is the total profit or revenue a business expects to earn from one customer over the whole time they keep buying, and it is often compared with CAC (customer acquisition cost).
Something that makes a business hard for competitors to copy, such as a brand, a patent, or a cost advantage.
MOQ (minimum order quantity) is the smallest order a factory or supplier will accept.
An MVP (minimum viable product) is a basic first version of a product, released to learn whether people want it before investing more.
The group of grocery stores focused on natural and organic foods, such as Whole Foods, Sprouts, and independent co-ops.
How many days a buyer has to pay an invoice. Net 30 means payment is due 30 days after the goods are delivered.
How long it takes for the money spent winning a customer, or on an investment, to be earned back.
The earliest formal round of outside money, often used to build a first product or test an idea.
Products made by one company and sold under another company's brand name, such as a store's own brand.
The point at which a product meets a need for a group of customers who buy it and keep using it.
A schedule that sets when and where a brand's products will be on sale or featured in stores over the year.
The number of individual store locations that carry a product. Being in 500 doors means being sold in 500 stores.
A projection of yearly sales based on a recent period. For example, $100,000 in one month is a $1.2 million annual run rate.
How many months a company can keep operating before it runs out of cash, at its current rate of spending.
An SBA loan is a small business loan that is partly guaranteed by the U.S. Small Business Administration, so the business repays it with interest without giving up ownership.
An early round of investment that helps a young company prove its idea works and start growing. It usually comes before a Series A.
The share of the products a store bought that sold to shoppers during a given period.
A round of venture investment that usually comes after the seed round. Later rounds are lettered B, C, and so on.
Describes a product that can be stored at room temperature without refrigeration until it is opened.
A SKU (stock keeping unit) is a unique code for one specific version of a product, such as one flavor in one size.
Payments a brand makes to a store chain, in cash or free product, to get its product placed on the shelf.
SRP (suggested retail price), or MSRP (manufacturer's suggested retail price), is the shelf price a brand recommends that stores charge.
TAM (total addressable market) is the total amount of money that could be spent on a product if every possible customer bought it.
Custom molds, dies, and equipment a factory needs to make a specific product. It is a large upfront cost paid before the first unit is made.
A TPR (temporary price reduction) is a short-term price cut on a product in a store, usually funded by the brand.
Money a brand spends to promote its products inside stores, such as price cuts, ads in store flyers, and display fees.
UNFI (United Natural Foods, Inc.) and KeHE Distributors are the two largest U.S. wholesale distributors that supply natural and specialty grocery stores.
How much money a business makes or loses on a single unit, like one product sold or one customer served, after the direct costs of making and delivering it. It is also the name of this show.
What a company is judged to be worth, usually agreed on during a fundraise or sale. It sets how much ownership an investor gets for their money.
How fast a product sells in each store, often measured as units sold per store per week.
Firms that invest pooled money from others into young companies in exchange for ownership.
The cash a business needs on hand to cover day-to-day costs such as inventory and bills while it waits to get paid for sales.
